title: Rabbi Tanchum bar Yirmeyah
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He is mentioned in the Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot, end of chapter 4, and the end of Maaserot.

It is related in Jerusalem Talmud Gittin, chapter 1, end of halakhah 2, that he was in the town of Chefer and issued a ruling there. They said to him: “Did not our master teach us that a student is forbidden to rule on a halakhah before his teacher unless he is twelve mil away? And here is Rabbi Mana, our master, sitting in Tzippori!” He said to them: “May it come upon me, for I did not know.” In Sanhedrin 5b it is cited: “Rabbi Tanchum son of Rabbi Ami came to Chatar and expounded for them … They said to him: Is not Rabbi Mani of Tyre here? He said to them: It did not occur to me.”

In Jerusalem Talmud Sheviit 6:1 the incident is told of Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya; in Tanchuma, Acharei 6, the reading is Rabbi Nachum bar Yirmeyah; and in Vayikra Rabbah 20:7 the reading is as in Jerusalem Talmud Gittin. Hyman considers it clear that the Jerusalem Talmud Gittin reading is correct, for one cannot say as in the Sheviit reading, since it is known that Rabbi Tanchum bar Chiyya was Rabbi Simon’s student, as explained in his entry — how then would he be Rabbi Mana’s student? Nor can one say that it is the first Rabbi Mana, since this Rabbi Mana was in Tiberias and not in Tzippori. As for the difficulty that Rabbi Mana was in Tzippori, it is no difficulty at all, for in fact he was almost all his days in Tiberias, the place of his father Rabbi Yonah and his teacher Rabbi Yose, and he also always went to Caesarea; only in his old age did he go to Tzippori, the place of Rabbi Chanina, who was the head there. Rabbi Chanina waived his honor for him, and Rabbi Mana was appointed head; therefore Rabbi Tanchum bar Yirmeyah did not know of this. He regards this as clear.
For the Tanchuma Hyman proposes Rabbi Tanchum instead of Rabbi Nachum.
A homily of his is mentioned in Bereshit Rabbah 3:8.

notes.text: ובסהדרין is read as Sanhedrin. The town and name variants Chefer/Chatar, Tanchum/Nachum and barYirmeyah/barChiyya/barAmi are retained. Hyman’s confident chronology, late move of Mana and proposed Tanchum correction remain his argument, with its clear and always force preserved.

The consulted Sanhedrin 5b names Tanchum son of Ami, Chater and Mani of Tyre and gives the rule in parasangs; the supplied Jerusalem Talmud account has twelve mil and its own names. These named alternatives do not establish identity by themselves. Hyman’s clear chronology, Mana I/II distinction, always-going claim and proposed Tanchum/Nachum correction retain their force as his reconstruction.
